name: Gibrat's Law
statement: A firm's growth rate does not depend on how big it already is.
statementAccent: does not depend on how big it already is
meaning: The proportional, or percentage, rate of growth of a firm (or a city) is independent of its absolute size. Whether an enterprise is tiny or huge, it has the same expected percentage growth and the same spread of possible outcomes. Growth is treated as a size-independent random draw applied to current size, so who ends up large is the cumulative result of many independent lucky and unlucky shocks.
mechanism: Model size as multiplied each period by a random factor drawn independently of current size. Taking logarithms turns the process into a sum of many independent random increments, and by the central limit theorem that sum tends toward a normal distribution, so the logarithm of size becomes normal and size itself lognormal. Repeated proportional random growth is the standard generative story for the lognormal size distributions seen across firms and cities.

examples.text: Gibrat drew the law from French industrial firms of the 1920s, whose size distribution was approximately lognormal: the empirical basis of his 1931 book.

Eeckhout's 2004 study found that the full distribution of United States city sizes is lognormal rather than a power law, consistent with proportionate Gibrat-style growth, with Zipf's law fitting only the largest cities.
Because multiplicative random growth generates lognormals, the law offers a mechanism for why firm and city sizes are so often lognormally distributed rather than clustered around an average.

variants.name: The lognormal distribution
variants.text: The size distribution that pure multiplicative random growth produces, and the reason lognormals recur across firm and settlement sizes.

variants.name: Zipf's law and the rank-size rule
variants.text: The competing power-law regularity that holds in the upper tail of city and firm sizes; a reflecting barrier or entry and exit can make Gibrat-type growth generate Zipf behaviour in the tail.

whyItMatters: It is a foundational null model for how firms and cities grow and why their sizes are so unequally distributed. As a baseline of pure proportionate growth, it frames the central empirical questions of industrial and urban economics, and the ways real data depart from it are themselves informative.

working.lead: Use it as a growth baseline
working.text: treat size-independent proportional growth as the null hypothesis, then test whether real firms or cities deviate from it.
where growth is roughly multiplicative and size-independent, anticipate a lognormal spread of sizes rather than a typical size.

working.lead: Watch the small and the surviving
working.text: remember the law fits large surviving firms better than small young ones, which tend to grow faster and exit more often.

limits: The law is empirically contested, especially for firms. Evidence repeatedly shows smaller firms grow faster than larger ones and are more likely to exit, contradicting strict size-independence; survivorship bias makes the law look better when only surviving firms are studied. Growth depends on age and other characteristics too. It survives better as a long-run regularity and for large, established firms. The city-size version is also disputed: the largest cities follow a power law rather than lognormal, leaving the whole-distribution question unsettled. The law functions best as a useful null model of proportionate growth rather than an established regularity.
misreadings: It does not claim all firms grow at the same rate, only that the expected percentage growth does not depend on size; actual growth is a random draw. And the evidence does not confirm it as an iron law: at the firm level the record runs mostly against strict size-independence in the short run.
origin: Proposed by the French engineer and economist Robert Gibrat in his 1931 book Les Inegalites economiques, drawing on French industrial firm data, as the law of proportionate effect.

sources.text: Gibrat's law, Wikipedia. — the size-independent-growth statement, the lognormal mechanism, and the firm-level evidence against it.
Eeckhout, "Gibrat's Law for (All) Cities," American Economic Review 94(5):1429-1451 (2004). — the lognormal city-size result and the Zipf-tail contrast.
